screens.title: Continuous Integration & Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll ground you in what CI, CD, and Continuous Deployment are and why a pragmatic programmer treats automation as a core craft. You will learn the practical purpose of each term, how they build on one another, and the concrete benefits they deliver: faster feedback, fewer integration surprises, and safer, smaller releases. We’ll look at the typical pipeline stages—source, build, test, deploy—and a short, hands-on GitHub Actions demo so you can see the automation in action. You’ll also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as slow tests or missing lock files, and sensible safety practices like isolated environments and rollback strategies. By the end of this module you should be able to describe when to aim for Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment, set up a basic CI workflow for a small Node. js project, and apply pragmatic checks so automation becomes a reliability tool rather than a liability. Think about the last stressful release you had and how automation could have made it smaller and sooner.

screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical capabilities you can use immediately. First, you will learn to explain the core ideas behind Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment. That means being able to name the difference: CI is frequent automated integration and testing, CD makes the artifact ready for release, and Continuous Deployment automatically pushes passing changes to production. Second, you will identify the essential pipeline stages: source, build, test, and deploy, and explain the purpose of artifacts and environments. You will also learn to configure a basic CI pipeline. The walkthrough uses a simple Node. js example and a GitHub Actions workflow so you can replicate it in your own projects. Finally, you will appreciate the pragmatic benefits of these practices: faster feedback, less risky releases, and higher software quality. Each objective includes a small mnemonic so you can remember the sequence and a verified competency milestone to guide practice. In short, you'll come away able to describe, set up, and reason about CI/CD in real projects.

screens.title: What is Continuous Integration (CI)?
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration is a disciplined development practice where developers frequently merge their work into a shared repository and each merge triggers an automated build and test run. The key claim is that small, frequent integrations catch integration issues early when they are cheapest to fix. A concrete example: two developers make related changes and push multiple times a day; a CI server runs the build and unit tests on each push, immediately surfacing a regression so the responsible change can be fixed before it reaches the mainline. In practice this means you keep the main branch in a releasable state and avoid long, painful merges. A common misconception is thinking CI is just a nightly build; that misses the point — CI should run on every push or pull request to provide timely feedback. To be pragmatic, ensure tests in CI are fast and focused so developers don’t bypass them. Key checks include compiling, running unit tests, and static analysis. Takeaway: CI is not a luxury—it's the minimal automation that prevents integration hell. Ask yourself: do your builds run often enough to catch errors before they ripple through the team?

Definition & Purpose
Developers integrate frequently and each change triggers an automated verification to detect integration problems early.
Why it matters

Example: Frequent merges with CI

screens.title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment are often confused, but the difference is important in practice. Both build on Continuous Integration: they ensure the software is always ready to release, but they differ in the final step. Continuous Delivery guarantees that every change that passes automated verification is prepared for release and can be deployed with a single manual action. Continuous Deployment removes that manual gate and pushes every passing change straight to production automatically. A concrete scenario: a team pushes changes that pass all CI checks and are deployed to staging; under Continuous Delivery a release manager or a manual trigger promotes the artifact to production, allowing human coordination and an extra check before high-impact releases. Under Continuous Deployment that same artifact flows to production without manual approval. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment eliminates responsibility; in fact it requires stronger test confidence and monitoring. Ask yourself: do you need business-level coordination for each release, or can you accept immediate production changes when tests and observability are mature? Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment means continuous delivery means 'ready to release'; continuous deployment means 'released automatically'—choose based on risk and business needs.. In practical terms, when you keep a manual gate and when you automate the final push. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Delivery vs Deployment
Continuous Delivery
Software is always in a deployable state; production deployment is a manual step or single click.
  • Automated builds and tests prepare artifacts for release.
  • Manual approval provides a human gate for coordination.
  • Useful when business timing or extra checks are required.
Example
Deploy to staging automatically; production requires a release click by the manager.
Continuous Deployment
Every change that passes automated pipelines is automatically deployed to production without human action.
  • Requires strong automated tests and monitoring.
  • Makes releases frequent and nearly invisible.
  • Best for low-risk, high-velocity teams with strong safety nets.
Example
Passing changes flow through staging and then to production automatically.
Practical guidance
Choose Continuous Delivery when you need human coordination or extra business checks. Choose Continuous Deployment when automated tests, feature flags, and monitoring give you confidence to release automatically. A hybrid strategy is common: automate everything up to a promotion, and automate production later once confidence grows.

screens.title: Typical CI/CD Pipeline Stages
screens.narratorSegment: A typical CI/CD pipeline follows a small set of stages that together move code from version control to a deployable artifact and then to an environment. Stage one is Source: a git push or pull request triggers the pipeline. Stage two is Build: the system resolves dependencies and produces artifacts such as JARs, Docker images, or minified bundles. Stage three is Test: automated suites run unit tests, integration checks, and static analysis; some teams also include limited end-to-end tests at this stage. Stage four is Deploy: the artifact is deployed to staging and then, depending on your practice, promoted to production. A concrete artifact example is a Docker image tagged with a build number used across environments, ensuring the same image runs in staging and production. A common error is coupling environment-specific configuration into the artifact rather than using environment variables and separate configuration, which causes inconsistencies between environments. To be pragmatic, separate build outputs from environment configuration, cache dependencies for speed, and fail fast when critical tests fail. Reflect: does your pipeline produce an artifact you can deploy unchanged between environments?

screens.title: Build Server, Jobs, Steps, and Artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: CI systems organize automation into workflows that the tool runs on a runner or build server. In this model, a workflow contains one or more jobs, each job runs on the same runner and is a group of sequential steps. A step is a single task such as checking out code, installing dependencies, running a command, or uploading an artifact. Artifacts are the outputs of builds—compiled binaries, Docker images, or static bundles—that subsequent jobs or deploy stages consume. For example, a workflow might have a build job that creates a Docker image and uploads it as an artifact, then a separate deploy job pulls that exact artifact and deploys it to staging. A common confusion is expecting steps in different jobs to share filesystem state; instead, pass artifacts between jobs or use a shared registry. Practically, define small jobs with clear responsibilities, use artifact storage to move outputs between jobs, and tag artifacts with build identifiers to ensure you deploy exactly what was built. Think about your current CI setup: are jobs too large and doing too many unrelated steps?

keyIdea.text: Workflows contain jobs; jobs contain steps; artifacts are the immutable outputs used later—design jobs to be focused and share artifacts explicitly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Build Server & Jobs
Concepts
  • Workflow: a defined sequence of jobs and triggers.
  • Job: runs on a single runner and groups sequential steps.
  • Step: a command or action, like checkout, install, test.
  • Artifact: build outputs stored for later use or deployment.
Misconception
Steps in different jobs do not share the runner filesystem; to move outputs use artifacts or registries instead of trying to copy files across jobs implicitly.
Tip

Keep jobs focused, pass artifacts explicitly, and tag artifacts with build ids so deployments are reproducible.

Example architecture
Job: build
Checkout → Install → Build → Upload artifact (image or bundle)
Job: test
Checkout → Download artifact → Run integration tests
Job: deploy
Download artifact → Deploy to staging → Notify
// Artifacts are immutable build outputs identified by tags or ids. // This ensures the deploy job uses the exact image built earlier.

screens.title: Testing Strategies in CI
screens.narratorSegment: Testing strategy is central to a pragmatic CI pipeline. The main idea is to balance speed and confidence: unit tests should be fast and run on every push to give immediate feedback. Integration tests validate interactions between components and can run in a secondary gate or as part of a scheduled pipeline if they are slower. End-to-end tests provide high confidence but are often slow and brittle, so reserve them for key release gates or run them selectively. A concrete example: run unit tests on every push, run integration tests on pull request merges or nightly, and run a small set of smoke end-to-end tests on staging for critical flows. A common mistake is leaving slow or flaky tests in the main gate; this causes developers to ignore failures or bypass CI, defeating its purpose. To avoid that, measure test durations, mark long tests as integration or E2E, and use test parallelization and caching. Final takeaway: keep the quick checks in the fast path and move expensive checks to well-defined gates so CI remains useful and kept green. Testing Strategies in CI means put fast tests in the main gate and move slower, brittle tests to secondary gates to keep ci responsive and trusted.. In practical terms, fast unit tests, selective integration tests, and where e2e fits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Testing Strategy
Testing tiers
Unit tests (fast)
Run on every push for immediate feedback.
Integration tests (medium)
Run on PR merge or nightly to validate component interaction.
End-to-end (slow)
Run a small smoke set in staging; full suites run less frequently.
Common problems & remediations
  • Slow tests: identify and move to secondary gates or parallelize them.
  • Flaky tests: quarantine and fix; flaky tests reduce trust in CI.
  • Missing test coverage for critical flows: add targeted smoke tests for production-significant paths.
Practical example
Run unit tests in the CI main job, run integration tests as a follow-up job, and run smoke E2E on staging before release.
Check
Are your slow tests blocking rapid feedback? If yes, reorganize them into secondary gates.

screens.title: GitHub Actions: A Minimal Node.js CI Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal GitHub Actions workflow for a Node. js project and explain the purpose of each section. First, the file declares a workflow name and triggers under an on field; this tells GitHub Actions when to run, for example on push or pull requests to main or develop. Jobs define units of work; the build job runs on a virtual machine. Steps are executed in order: checkout fetches repository code, setup-node prepares the runtime, install uses npm ci to install exact dependency versions, test runs the test script, and build runs an optional build step. Using npm ci depends on committing a lock file; if the lock file is missing the install will fail. The reason to separate steps is clarity and reusability: you can cache dependencies between runs or reuse actions like checkout and setup-node. A common learner error is committing a workflow with uncommitted lock files. Always commit lock files and verify that the test script returns a proper exit code so the job fails on test errors. After watching the YAML example try creating this workflow in a simple repository to see the pipeline run.

keyIdea.title: YAML roles
keyIdea.text: on triggers the workflow; jobs group steps; steps perform actions like checkout, setup runtime, install, test, and build.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › GitHub Actions Walkthrough
YAML explained
Name and triggers control when the workflow runs. Jobs run on runners and contain steps executed in order.
  • Use actions for common tasks like checkout and runtime setup.
  • Use npm ci for reproducible installs and commit package-lock.json.
  • Fail early if tests return a non-zero exit to avoid false green builds.
Key example note
If install fails because package-lock.json is missing, add and commit the lock file, then re-run CI.
# .github/workflows/node-ci.yml
name: Node.js CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, develop ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20.x' # Specify the Node.js version

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci # 'ci' installs dependencies from package-lock.json, ensuring consistent builds

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test # Assumes you have a 'test' script in your package.json

    - name: Build project (if applicable)
      run: npm run build --if-present # Runs 'build' script if it exists

screens.title: Secrets, Environments, and Rollbacks
screens.narratorSegment: Security and operational safety are essential in CI/CD. Never embed secrets or credentials in repository code. Instead, store them in the CI tool's secrets store or a secure secret manager and reference them at runtime. Use distinct environments—development, staging, and production—with appropriate access controls to avoid configuration drift. A pragmatic rollback strategy is also critical: tag and store artifacts so you can redeploy a known-good version quickly if a release proves faulty. A simple rollback plan is to keep the previous artifact in the registry or artifact store and script a redeploy step that targets the earlier tag. A common mistake is relying on manual file edits or database changes without versioned artifacts; this makes rollbacks hard or impossible. Also, scope permissions for CI runners and tokens to the minimum needed and rotate secrets regularly. The takeaway: treat deployment as an automated, reversible operation—secure secrets, isolate environments, and ensure quick redeploy paths for safe recovery. Secrets, Environments, and Rollbacks means store secrets securely, isolate environments, tag artifacts, and have scripted rollbacks so deployments are reversible and auditable.. In practical terms, keeping credentials safe, managing stages, and planning safe rollbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Secrets
Use the CI provider's secret store or an external secrets manager. Reference secrets at runtime, never commit them to source control.
Limit token scopes and rotate credentials regularly to reduce exposure.
Environments
Keep development, staging, and production isolated and configure environment-specific settings outside the artifact.
Use feature flags if you need gradual exposure without multiple deploys.
Rollback
Tag and store artifacts so you can redeploy a known-good version quickly when needed.
Script the redeploy path and test it so rollbacks aren’t ad-hoc operations during an incident.

screens.title: Common CI/CD Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Pragmatic teams watch for a handful of common mistakes that erode CI/CD value. Slow tests are the most frequent problem; when pipelines take too long, developers avoid them. The remedy is to split tests by speed and importance: fast unit tests in the main gate, longer integration or E2E tests in secondary gates. A second issue is ignoring failing pipelines: teams sometimes treat a red build as normal. This creates technical debt; keep the pipeline green by fixing failures promptly and making the owner visible. Third, missing lock files cause non-reproducible installs and failures such as npm ci errors; always commit package-lock. json or equivalent. Fourth, environment drift occurs when configuration lives in code or local machines instead of being applied at deploy time; separate configuration from artifacts to keep environments consistent. To close, adopt a cultural rule: a failing pipeline blocks merges until fixed, and automate fast signals so developers can restore green status quickly. Slow tests

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Set up a Basic Node.js CI
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a simple Node. js project, committing a minimal test script, and adding a GitHub Actions workflow so a pipeline runs on push. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll ground you in what CI, CD, and Continuous Deployment are and why a pragmatic programmer treats automation as a core craft. You will learn the practical purpose of each term, how they build on one another, and the concrete benefits they deliver: faster feedback, fewer integration surprises, and safer, smaller releases. We’ll look at the typical pipeline stages—source, build, test, deploy—and a short, hands-on GitHub Actions demo so you can see the automation in action. You’ll also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as slow tests or missing lock files, and sensible safety practices like isolated environments and rollback strategies. By the end of this module you should be able to describe when to aim for Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment, set up a basic CI workflow for a small Node. js project, and apply pragmatic checks so automation becomes a reliability tool rather than a liability. Think about the last stressful release you had and how automation could have made it smaller and sooner.

These learning objectives map to practical capabilities you can use immediately. First, you will learn to explain the core ideas behind Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment. That means being able to name the difference: CI is frequent automated integration and testing, CD makes the artifact ready for release, and Continuous Deployment automatically pushes passing changes to production. Second, you will identify the essential pipeline stages: source, build, test, and deploy, and explain the purpose of artifacts and environments. You will also learn to configure a basic CI pipeline. The walkthrough uses a simple Node. js example and a GitHub Actions workflow so you can replicate it in your own projects. Finally, you will appreciate the pragmatic benefits of these practices: faster feedback, less risky releases, and higher software quality. Each objective includes a small mnemonic so you can remember the sequence and a verified competency milestone to guide practice. In short, you'll come away able to describe, set up, and reason about CI/CD in real projects.

This second objectives slide ties each learning outcome to daily developer tasks. Knowing the difference between CI, CD, and Continuous Deployment changes how you branch and commit: frequent small merges make integration issues visible quickly. Understanding pipeline stages changes how you write and measure tests: unit tests stay fast to keep CI quick, integration tests run where they add value, and end-to-end tests are reserved for narrower gates. Being able to set up a GitHub Actions workflow means you can automate those checks so you and your team get immediate feedback on each push. Finally, adopting pragmatic safety measures — committing lock files, isolating staging environments, and defining rollback steps — turns deployment from a risky ceremony into a routine operation. Each objective is chosen to be directly useful: faster feedback, fewer release surprises, and more confident teams. Prepare to practice a hands-on lab where you will create a Node. js repository, add the workflow YAML, push to GitHub, and observe an actual pipeline run in the repository's Actions tab.

Continuous Integration is a disciplined development practice where developers frequently merge their work into a shared repository and each merge triggers an automated build and test run. The key claim is that small, frequent integrations catch integration issues early when they are cheapest to fix. A concrete example: two developers make related changes and push multiple times a day; a CI server runs the build and unit tests on each push, immediately surfacing a regression so the responsible change can be fixed before it reaches the mainline. In practice this means you keep the main branch in a releasable state and avoid long, painful merges. A common misconception is thinking CI is just a nightly build; that misses the point — CI should run on every push or pull request to provide timely feedback. To be pragmatic, ensure tests in CI are fast and focused so developers don’t bypass them. Key checks include compiling, running unit tests, and static analysis. Takeaway: CI is not a luxury—it's the minimal automation that prevents integration hell. Ask yourself: do your builds run often enough to catch errors before they ripple through the team?

Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment are often confused, but the difference is important in practice. Both build on Continuous Integration: they ensure the software is always ready to release, but they differ in the final step. Continuous Delivery guarantees that every change that passes automated verification is prepared for release and can be deployed with a single manual action. Continuous Deployment removes that manual gate and pushes every passing change straight to production automatically. A concrete scenario: a team pushes changes that pass all CI checks and are deployed to staging; under Continuous Delivery a release manager or a manual trigger promotes the artifact to production, allowing human coordination and an extra check before high-impact releases. Under Continuous Deployment that same artifact flows to production without manual approval. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment eliminates responsibility; in fact it requires stronger test confidence and monitoring. Ask yourself: do you need business-level coordination for each release, or can you accept immediate production changes when tests and observability are mature? Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment means continuous delivery means 'ready to release'; continuous deployment means 'released automatically'—choose based on risk and business needs.. In practical terms, when you keep a manual gate and when you automate the final push. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A typical CI/CD pipeline follows a small set of stages that together move code from version control to a deployable artifact and then to an environment. Stage one is Source: a git push or pull request triggers the pipeline. Stage two is Build: the system resolves dependencies and produces artifacts such as JARs, Docker images, or minified bundles. Stage three is Test: automated suites run unit tests, integration checks, and static analysis; some teams also include limited end-to-end tests at this stage. Stage four is Deploy: the artifact is deployed to staging and then, depending on your practice, promoted to production. A concrete artifact example is a Docker image tagged with a build number used across environments, ensuring the same image runs in staging and production. A common error is coupling environment-specific configuration into the artifact rather than using environment variables and separate configuration, which causes inconsistencies between environments. To be pragmatic, separate build outputs from environment configuration, cache dependencies for speed, and fail fast when critical tests fail. Reflect: does your pipeline produce an artifact you can deploy unchanged between environments?

CI systems organize automation into workflows that the tool runs on a runner or build server. In this model, a workflow contains one or more jobs, each job runs on the same runner and is a group of sequential steps. A step is a single task such as checking out code, installing dependencies, running a command, or uploading an artifact. Artifacts are the outputs of builds—compiled binaries, Docker images, or static bundles—that subsequent jobs or deploy stages consume. For example, a workflow might have a build job that creates a Docker image and uploads it as an artifact, then a separate deploy job pulls that exact artifact and deploys it to staging. A common confusion is expecting steps in different jobs to share filesystem state; instead, pass artifacts between jobs or use a shared registry. Practically, define small jobs with clear responsibilities, use artifact storage to move outputs between jobs, and tag artifacts with build identifiers to ensure you deploy exactly what was built. Think about your current CI setup: are jobs too large and doing too many unrelated steps?

Testing strategy is central to a pragmatic CI pipeline. The main idea is to balance speed and confidence: unit tests should be fast and run on every push to give immediate feedback. Integration tests validate interactions between components and can run in a secondary gate or as part of a scheduled pipeline if they are slower. End-to-end tests provide high confidence but are often slow and brittle, so reserve them for key release gates or run them selectively. A concrete example: run unit tests on every push, run integration tests on pull request merges or nightly, and run a small set of smoke end-to-end tests on staging for critical flows. A common mistake is leaving slow or flaky tests in the main gate; this causes developers to ignore failures or bypass CI, defeating its purpose. To avoid that, measure test durations, mark long tests as integration or E2E, and use test parallelization and caching. Final takeaway: keep the quick checks in the fast path and move expensive checks to well-defined gates so CI remains useful and kept green. In practical terms, fast unit tests, selective integration tests, and where e2e fits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
